newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba council meets in Bavaria amid EMU debate.
newsitem.headline: Buba council meets in Bavaria amid EMU debate.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Thursday began in its annual out-of-town council meeting in the small Bavarian town of Aschau with most economists predicting the bank will keep its interest rates unchanged.
The bank has scheduled a news conference for 1015 GMT, as is usual after its meetings outside Frankfurt.

Financial markets are waiting for comments from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer on prospects for European economic and monetary union (EMU), the recent appreciation of the dollar, and the outlook for German interest rates.
This year's meeting in Aschau, a picturesque town nestling in the foothills of the Alps, comes at a time of fierce debate within Germany about the introduction if the planned single currency.

During a reception here on Wednesday evening, Tietmeyer appeared to try to rein in Bavarian Premier Edmund Stoiber, who has spearheaded a campaign calling for the strictest possible interpretation of the EMU convergence criteria.

His remarks have cast doubt on whether the euro will be launched punctually and this week contributed to pressure on the mark on the foreign exchange markets as investors opted for safe havens from euro uncertainty. The mark was trading at 1.7628 to the dollar at 0840 GMT.
Adressing Stoiber, who hosted the reception, Tietmeyer said the premier had been right to insist that the pre-conditions for entry into monetary union must be right.

But, in an apparent reference to Stoiber's call that nations' budget deficits must not be allowed to exceed 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, Tietmeyer said: "I have the impression that the zero discussion has obscured the substance of the issue."
He noted that both houses of the federal parliament had as early as December 1992 stressed the need for nations to prove that their budgets and economic convergence were sustainable.
The Maastricht treaty, which lays down the three percent ceiling for nations seeking to qualify for the euro, allows a certain overshoot in special circumstances.

Many independent economists doubt that Germany will be able to get its budget deficit down to 3.0 percent or lower but they, as well as a number of Bundesbank officials, have stressed that the Treaty allows leeway in interpretation.
In addition, France recently said that its deficit in 1997 will be much higher than 3.0 percent.
